summary_note: Ten atomic documentary and interpretive claims for Case 3300 (bogus, TGT-004) covering all 70 agent-verified citations across the 1847 Secret Band of Brothers dating calibration, 1825–1842 apparatus-to-sham chronology, four 1853–1889 derivative antedatings, competing tantrabogus/calibogus donor pathways, and falsified folk myths.

claims.short_label: Falsification of the alleged "c. 1798 Band of Brothers" baseline to Jonathan H. Green's 1846–1847 composition
claims.statement: The alleged "c. 1798" Band of Brothers quotation ("Coney means Counterfeit paper money ... Bogus means spurious coin") cited in HDAS (1994), World Wide Words (2000), and Grammarphobia (2014) is not an 18th-century text, but Chapter XII (p. 113) of Jonathan Harrington Green's spring 1847 book The Secret Band of Brothers, exposed as an 1846–1847 composition by statutory, toponymic, serial, and lexical anachronisms.
claims.rationale: Congress did not create the 'Western District of Virginia' named in the p. 90 charter header until Feb. 4, 1819 (3 Stat. 478); Chapter XII letters dated '1825' cite post-1834 'Toronto' and post-1835 'Manhattan, Ohio'; Chapters I–X were serialized July–Sept. 1846 in The Casket; Green admitted post-charter vocabulary additions on p. 112 and printed identical footnotes in Gambling Unmasked! (1847); and clipped 'Coney' postdates 1823 'Cogniac' and 1836 'coniackers'.

evidence_boundary.establishes: That Secret Band of Brothers p. 113 was composed and published in 1846–1847 and cannot serve as a 1798 attestation of bogus or coney.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Whether oral counterfeiters' cant used bogus locally prior to 1825–1827 without surviving print witnesses.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Exact informants from whom J. H. Green gathered his 1840s Ohio and Mississippi Valley flash vocabulary.

limitations: CERT-3300-201 cites the 2006 Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1858 T. B. Peterson stereotype reissue alongside 1846–1847 primary serial and companion-book scans in CERT-3300-202 through CERT-3300-204.

evidence.reason: Full text of Chapter XII pp. 90, 112–113, 122, 125 exposing internal anachronisms and p. 112 editorial admission.
Sept. 16, 1846 Casket editorial announcing original July–Sept. 1846 serialization and withholding of the Constitution/By-Laws.
March 13, 1847 National Police Gazette G. B. Zieber & Co. pre-publication advertisement ('now in press').
1847 Gambling Unmasked! p. 123 printing Green's identical 1847 footnotes defining 'Coney' and 'Bogus'.
U.S. Statutes at Large Vol. III p. 478 proving Virginia's Western District was created Feb. 4, 1819, 21 years after 'July 12, 1798'.
1823 Coffey Inside Out p. 108 showing NY prisoners still used unclipped 'imported Cogniac' (0x coney, 0x bogus).
Oct. 11, 1836 Missiskoui Standard p. 3 attesting unclipped 'coniackers' in Lower Canada.

claims.case_section: Pre-Painesville Onomastic Precursor and the 1827–1833 Coining Apparatus

claims.statement: Primary scans document a February 19, 1825 Ohio Valley rag-money satirical stage sobriquet 'Bogus' (for KY Attorney General Solomon P. Sharp), followed by May–July 1827 Painesville counterfeiting-raid dispatches, Eber D. Howe's firsthand 1827 press account, and a September 3, 1833 Lower Canada seizure explicitly defining 'One bogus, or machine impressing dies on the coin'.
claims.rationale: Preserves strict Trap C separation between the 1825 proper stage name and the 1827–1833 common count noun designating a counterfeiter's cast-iron die press.

claims.case_section: Evaluating *Tantrabogus* vs. *Calibogus* and Rebutting Rival Folk Myths
claims.short_label: Comparative evaluation of aphetic New England tantrabogus ('ill-looking contraption') vs. maritime calibogus ('spruce beer and rum')
claims.statement: Both New England colloquial tantrabogus (attested orally in a 1759 Massachusetts journal, in 1838 Boston /ˌboʊɡəs/ rhyme, and in Dr. Samuel Willard's pre-1831 Vermont testimony, though never mentioned by Eber D. Howe in 1878) and North Atlantic cant calibogus (attested 1766–1811, with simplex beverage BOGUS first printed in Bartlett 1848) supply viable Northern phonological shapes, with semantics favoring tantrabogus for the 1827 cast-iron press while leaving oral convergence with calibogus open.
claims.rationale: Preserves scholarly candor: primary scans confirm pre-1827 oral currency for both donor stems while exposing both the Howe=Willard conflation and the 1811 'Cali BOGUS' OCR-split mirage.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Pre-1827 Northern currency of both tantrabogus (1759 MS, pre-1831 VT memory, 1838 rhyme) and calibogus (1766–1811), plus exact 1848 print debut of beverage BOGUS.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Direct metalinguistic witness of the clipping event prior to May–July 1827.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether 1825–1827 speakers clipped tantrabogus directly for the Painesville press or merged it with oral tavern calibogus/bogus.

limitations: Constantine Hardy's 1759 journal (CERT-3300-301) survives via a 1906 NEHGR antiquarian transcription, and Joseph Banks's 1766 Newfoundland journal (CERT-3300-309) via Lysaght's 1971 edition.
resolution_criteria: Discovery of a pre-1827 New England or Western Reserve manuscript, tavern ledger, or court deposition explicitly linking bogus either to tantrabogus ('contraption') or to calibogus/bogus ('adulterated liquor').

evidence.reason: 1759 Crown Point journal (pub. 1906 NEHGR) attesting Massachusetts soldier's oral 'tantrabogus' for Ticonderoga.

claims.short_label: Negative-corpus absence of bogus and coney across 1798–1844 Northeastern counterfeiting memoirs, prison glossaries, and bank-note detectors
claims.statement: Full-text primary-scan audits of Stephen Burroughs's Memoirs (1798), Henry Tufts's Dover 'Nomenclature of the Flash Language' (1807), William A. Coffey's NY State Prison Inside Out (1823), Bicknell's Counterfeit Detector (Feb. 1836), and Richard H. Phelps's Newgate of Connecticut (1844) yield zero occurrences of bogus or clipped coney.
claims.rationale: Bounds the geographic and chronological emergence of bogus: pre-1827 New England, New York, and Philadelphia counterfeiting literature relied exclusively on English flash ('lour', 'queer', 'imported Cogniac') before Western Reserve foundry slang ('bogus', 1827–1835) spread eastward.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Complete absence of bogus and coney across five canonical 1798–1844 Northeastern counterfeiting and prison-flash texts.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence in unprinted Western frontier speech prior to 1825–1827.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether manuscript county-court files in Vermont or Ohio preserve pre-1827 cant tokens.

limitations: Published memoirs and Eastern bank-note detectors reflect Northeastern print registers prior to the 1835–1838 Western currency-slang wave.

evidence.reason: 1798 Stephen Burroughs Memoirs (Hanover, NH) full-text negative control (0x bogus, 0x coney).
1807 Henry Tufts 'Nomenclature of the Flash Language' (1930 Pearson ed. w/ 1807 title facsimile) negative control (0x bogus).
